'''Jesse Ernest Wilkins Jr.''' (November 27, 1923 – May 1, 2011)<ref name="Tribune">Chicago Tribune. [http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/chicagotribune/obituary.aspx?n=j-ernest-wilkins&pid=150779097 Obituary: J. Ernest Wilkins], Chicago Tribune,  May 4, 2011.</ref> was an American [[Nuclear physics|nuclear scientist]], [[mechanical engineer]] and [[mathematician]].  A [[child prodigy]], he attended the [[University of Chicago]] at the age of 13, becoming its youngest ever student.<ref name="CBB"/><ref name="mad">Mathematicians of the African Diaspora. [http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/wilkns_jearnest.html J. Ernest Wilkins Jr.],  Department of Mathematics, University of Buffalo. Retrieved online May 7, 2011.</ref><ref name="DOE">U.S. Department Of Energy, [http://www.africanafrican.com/negroartist/writings/BLACK%20CONTRIBUTORS/BLACK%20CONTRIBUTORS_Page_09.jpg Black Contributors to Science and Energy Technology (Biographical sketch: Ernest Wilkins)], U.S. Department Of Energy, Office of Public Affairs, U.S.Government Printing Office, Washington, D.C., 1979, pp. 14–15, DOE/OPA-0035(79)</ref> His graduation at a young age resulted in him being hailed as "the Negro Genius" in the national media.<ref name="Farmer">{{cite book |last1=Farmer |first1=Vernon L. |last2=Shepherd-Wynn |first2=Evelyn |title=Voices of Historical and Contemporary Black American Pioneers (Volume I: Medicine and Science) |date=2012 |publisher=Praeger |page=35 |isbn=978-0313392252 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O8tEwW7E8PIC&pg=PA35 |access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref>

Wilkins and [[Eugene Wigner]] co-developed the Wigner-Wilkins approach for estimating the distribution of neutron energies within nuclear reactors, which is the basis for how all nuclear reactors are designed. Wilkins later went on to become the President of the American Nuclear Society in 1974.<ref>Atomic Heritage Foundation, 2019. https://www.atomicheritage.org/profile/j-ernest-wilkins-jr</ref>

Wilkins had a widely varied career, spanning seven decades and including significant contributions to pure and [[applied mathematics]], civil and nuclear engineering, and optics.<ref name="Mickens">{{cite journal |last1=Mickens |first1=Ronald E. |title=Obituary of J. Ernest Wilkins, Jr. (1923-2011) |journal=Physics Today |date=18 January 2013 |issue=1 |page=3234 |doi=10.1063/PT.4.1695 |bibcode=2013PhT..2013a3234. |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/PT.4.1695/full/ |access-date=27 February 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Wilkins was one of the [[African American scientists and technicians on the Manhattan Project]] during the [[Second World War]]. He also conducted [[nuclear physics]] research in both academia and industry. He wrote numerous scientific papers, served in various important posts, earned several significant awards and helped recruit [[Minority group|minority students]] into the sciences.<ref name="CBB"/><ref name="UofChicago">University of Chicago. [http://www-news.uchicago.edu/releases/07/070227.wilkins.shtml University of Chicago to Commemorate Accomplishments of Mathematics Alumnus J. Ernest Wilkins Jr. ], University of Chicago News Office, February 27, 2007, updated July 23, 2007. Retrieved June 9, 2011.</ref><ref name="UofChicagoMagazine">Y., M.R., University of Chicago Magazine. [http://uchiblogo.uchicago.edu/archives/2007/03/the_wilkins_eff.html The Wilkins Effect], University of Chicago, March 2, 2007. Retrieved June 9, 2011.</ref>  During his life he was often the target of racism.<ref name="CBB" />

== Education and early career ==

In 1940, Wilkins completed his [[Bachelor of Arts|AB]] in mathematics at the University of Chicago.<ref name="mad"/> He went on to an MS and PhD in mathematics at the same institution, which he completed in 1941 and 1942.<ref name="mad"/>  His thesis was titled ''Multiple Integral Problems in Parametric Form in the Calculus of Variations'', and was advised by [[Magnus Hestenes]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=6384|name= Jesse Ernest Wilkins, Jr.}}</ref>

Having initially been unable to secure a research position,<ref name="Alic"/> Wilkins taught mathematics from 1943 to 1944 at the [[Tuskegee University|Tuskegee Institute]] (now Tuskegee University) in Tuskegee, [[Alabama]].<ref name="mad"/>

== Manhattan Project ==
In 1944 Wilkins returned to the University of Chicago where he served first as an [[Mathematical physics|associate mathematical physicist]] and then as a [[physicist]] in its Metallurgical Laboratory, as part of the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name="DOE" /> Working under the direction of [[Arthur Holly Compton]] and [[Enrico Fermi]], Wilkins researched the extraction of fissionable nuclear materials, but was not told of the research group's ultimate goal until after the [[atomic bomb]] was dropped on [[Hiroshima]]. Wilkins was the co-discoverer or discoverer of a number of phenomena in physics such as the Wilkins effect and the Wigner–Wilkins spectra.<ref name="Gates">Gates, Henry Louis & Higginbotham, Evelyn Brooks. [https://books.google.com/books?id=3dXw6gR2GgkC&pg=PA883 African American Lives], Oxford University Press, U.S., 2004, pp. 883–884, {{ISBN|978-0195160246}}.</ref>

When Wilkins's team was about to be transferred to the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] in [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]] (known at the time as site "X"), due to the [[Jim Crow laws]] of the [[Southern United States]], Wilkins would have been prevented from working there. When [[Edward Teller]] was informed about this, he wrote a letter on September 18, 1944, to [[Harold Urey]] (who was the director of war research at Columbia at the time) of Wilkins's abilities, informing him about the issue caused by local reactions to Wilkins's race, and recommending his services for a new position.<ref name="Kiernan">{{cite book|title=The Girls of Atomic City: The Untold Story of the Women Who Helped Win World War II|date=2013|publisher=Simon and Schuster|isbn=978-1451617542|page=47|author=Denise Kiernan}}</ref> As Teller explained: {{cquote

|Knowing that men of high qualifications are scarce these days, I thought that it might be useful that I suggest a capable person for this job. Mr. Wilkins in Wigner's group at the Metallurgical Laboratory has been doing, according to Wigner, excellent work. He is a colored man and since Wigner's group is moving to "X" it is not possible for him to continue work with that group. I think that it might be a good idea to secure his services for our work.<ref>{{cite web
 |title        = Edward Teller Letter Concerning Black Mathematician
 |url          = http://nationalarchivesatlanta.omeka.net/items/show/147
 |publisher    = The National Archives at Atlanta
 |access-date  = 9 February 2014
 |url-status   = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222155959/http://nationalarchivesatlanta.omeka.net/items/show/147
 |archive-date = 22 February 2014
 }}</ref>}}

Wilkins then continued to teach mathematics and conduct significant research in neutron absorption with physicist [[Eugene Wigner]], including the development of its mathematical models.<ref name="CBB"/><ref name="DOE" />  He would also later help design and develop [[nuclear reactor]]s for electrical [[power generation]], becoming part owner of one such company.<ref name="DOE" />

== Later career ==
[[File:J. Ernest Wilkins Jr. (short biographies and sketches- U.S. Gov'mt -GPO) V2 -cropped-.jpg|thumb|250px|left|Sketch of Wilkins from a [http://www.africanafrican.com/negroartist/writings/BLACK%20CONTRIBUTORS/BLACK%20CONTRIBUTORS_Page_09.jpg U.S. Department of Energy biography]<ref name="DOE"/>]]

To improve communication between mathematicians and nuclear engineers on a project, Wilkins earned  bachelor's (1957) and master's degrees (1960) in mechanical engineering from [[New York University]], thus earning five science degrees during his life. It also qualified him to design and build nuclear facilities.<ref name="Alic">{{cite web |last1=Alic |first1=Margaret |title=Wilkins, J. Ernest Jr. 1923– |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/education/news-wires-white-papers-and-books/wilkins-j-ernest-jr-1923 |website=Contemporary Black Biography: Encyclopedia.com |access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref>

In 1970 Wilkins went on to serve [[Howard University]] as its distinguished professor of [[Applied mathematics#Divisions of applied mathematics|applied mathematical physics]] and also to help found the university's PhD program in mathematics.<ref name="DOE" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ortega|first1=Omayra|last2=Lawrence|first2=Emille Davie |last3=Goins|first3=Edray Herber|title=The Golden Anniversary Celebration of the National Association of Mathematicians|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jsQOEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA7|year= 2020|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-1470451301|page=177}}</ref> During his tenure at Howard he undertook a sabbatical position as a visiting scientist at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] from 1976 to 1977.<ref name="CBB"/>

From 1974 to 1975 Wilkins served as president of the [[American Nuclear Society]]<ref name="DOE" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Wilkins_Ernest.html|title=McTutor}}</ref> and in 1976 became the second African American to be elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]].<ref name="DOE" /><ref name="UC">Koppes, Steve. [http://www-news.uchicago.edu/releases/07/070227.wilkins.shtml University of Chicago to Commemorate Accomplishments of Mathematics Alumnus J. Ernest Wilkins Jr.] (media release), News Office, University of Chicago, February 27, 2007.</ref>
[[File:Shabazz Blackwell Wilkins.jpg|thumb|J. Ernest Wilkins Jr. (right) at the Conference for African American Researchers in the Mathematical Sciences (CAARMS), Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI), Berkeley, California in June 1995. Next to him are, from left to right: [[Abdulalim A. Shabazz|Abdulalim Shabazz]] and [[David Blackwell]].]]
From 1990 Wilkins lived and worked in [[Atlanta, Georgia]], as a [[distinguished professor]] of applied mathematics and [[mathematical physics]] at [[Clark Atlanta University]], and retired again for his last time in 2003.<ref name="CBB" /><ref name="UC" /> 

Throughout his years of research Wilkins published more than 100 papers on a variety of subjects, including [[differential geometry]], [[linear differential equation]]s, [[integrals]], [[nuclear engineering]], [[gamma radiation]] shielding and [[optics]], garnering numerous professional and scientific awards along the way.<ref name="CBB"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Ernst_J._Wilkins,_Jr.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120526025924/http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Ernst_J._Wilkins,_Jr.|url-status=dead|title=IEEE Biography: Wilkins Jr.|archivedate=May 26, 2012}}</ref>

== Family ==

Wilkins had two children with his first wife Gloria Louise Steward (d. 1980) whom he married in June 1947,<ref name="Tribune" /><ref name="Gates" /> married Maxine G. Malone in 1984. He was married a third time to Vera Wood Anderson in Chicago in September 2003. He had a daughter, Sharon, and a son, J. Ernest III, during his first marriage.<ref name="Mickens" /><ref name="Gates" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Wilkins_Ernest/|website=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]]|title=Jesse Ernest Wilkins Jr.|access-date=August 20, 2021}}</ref>

His father, [[J. Ernest Wilkins Sr.]], served as [[US Assistant Secretary of Labor]] during the [[Eisenhower administration]].<ref name="CBB">Zerbonia, Ralph G. (contrib. by Alic, Margaret) (2005) [https://books.google.com/books?ei=5LfxSezpMZHGzASv0KyVCw Contemporary Black Biography], Gale Research Inc, 2005, Vol. 49 (Original from the [[University of Michigan]]), Digitized September 17, 2008, {{ISBN|978-0787667313}}.</ref>

Wilkins is the uncle of two notable attorneys: [[David B. Wilkins]], a professor at the [[Harvard Law School]], and [[Timothy A. Wilkins]], a partner with [[Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Race, Sustainability, and Social Justice: A Conversation with the Wilkins Brothers|url=https://clp.law.harvard.edu/event-post/race-sustainability-and-social-justice-a-conversation-with-the-wilkins-brothers/|access-date=2021-05-27|website=Harvard CLP|language=en}}</ref> In 2010 a niece of Wilkins, Carolyn Marie Wilkins, Professor of Music at the [[Berklee College of Music]] in Boston, wrote of Wilkins' father and her family more generally in her biography ''Damn Near White: An African American Family's Rise from Slavery to Bittersweet Success''.<ref name="DamnNear">Wilkins, Carolyn Marie. [https://books.google.com/books?id=VUTE-ah3gaMC Damn Near White: An African American Family's Rise from Slavery to Bittersweet Success], University of Missouri Press, 2010, {{ISBN|978-0826218995}}.</ref>

== Death and legacy ==
Wilkins died on May 1, 2011, in Fountain Hills, Arizona.<ref name="Tribune" />  He was buried at the [[National Memorial Cemetery of Arizona|National Memorial Cemetery]], [[Cave Creek, Arizona]], on May 5.<ref name="Tribune" />

Wilkins is portrayed by Ronald Auguste in the 2023 film ''[[Oppenheimer (film)|Oppenheimer]]'',<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023 |title=Oppenheimer 2023 Full Cast and Crew |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt15398776/fullcredits/?ref_=tt_ql_1 |access-date=December 24, 2023 |website=IMDb}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Rayford |first=Rayna Reid |date=August 13, 2023 |title=Why Are We Still Whitewashing History In 2023? |work=Essence |url=https://www.essence.com/news/oppenheimer-whitewashed-history/ |access-date=December 24, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Thompson |first=David |date=August 1, 2023 |title=Full Cast of Oppenheimer: Every Main Actor & Who They Play |work=The Direct |url=https://thedirect.com/article/oppenheimer-cast-characters-actors |access-date=December 24, 2023}}</ref>  named one of the top-ten films of 2023 by the [[National Board of Review]] and the [[American Film Institute]].

== Tributes and honors ==
[[File:J. Ernest Wilkins, Jr. -University of Chicago dedication, March 2007 -No. 19.jpg|thumb|'''Wilkins portrait and plaque''' honoring him in the Eckhart Hall Tea Room of the Physical Sciences Division, University of Chicago in 2007 (courtesy: Dan Dry)]]
* The Wilkins effect, plus the [[Wigner–Wilkins spectrum|Wigner–Wilkins]] and Wilkins spectra, discovered during the 1940s, are named or co-named after him;<ref name="UofChicagoMagazine" />
* In March 2007 Wilkins was honored by his [[alma mater]], the [[University of Chicago]], in a special ceremony that included the dedication of his portrait and a plaque in the Eckhart Hall Tea Room of its Physical Sciences Division;<ref name="UofChicago" />
* U.S. Army Outstanding Civilian Service Medal, 1980;<ref name="Answers.com" />
* NAM, Honorary Life Member, Lifetime Achievement Award, 1994;<ref name="Answers.com" />
* QEM Network, Giant in Science Award, 1994;<ref name="Answers.com" />
* Department of Energy, Special Recognition Award, 1996;<ref name="Answers.com" />
* University of Chicago Alumni Association, Professional Achievement Citation, 1997.<ref name="Answers.com" />

== Memberships ==

Some of Wilkins's memberships included:
* [[Kappa Alpha Psi]] fraternity 1938<ref name="Answers.com">Alic, Margaret. [http://www.answers.com/topic/j-ernest-wilkins-jr J. Ernest Wilkins Jr.], [[Gale (publisher)|Gale Contemporary Black Biography]], 2006.  Retrieved from Answers.com</ref>
* [[National Academy of Engineering]], Member, elected in 1976;
* [[American Society of Mechanical Engineers]];
* [[American Nuclear Society]], Board of Directors, 1967–77, President, 1974–75;
* [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council of the United States]], Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, Chairman, 1990–94;
* [[Oak Ridge Associated Universities]], council, 1990;
* U.S. Army Science Board, chairman, 1970–2001.
* Original Forty Club of Chicago, Treasurer 1986; Secretary 1990 <ref>The Original Forty Club of Chicago: THE SEVENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY PUBLICATION</ref>
